title: IDVO’s $445 Million Income Play Faces a Critical Test When TSM Growth Slows - AOL.com
content: IDVO’s covered-call strategy faces pressure if volatile holdings like Taiwan Semiconductor cool off or get called away. Watch Taiwan Semiconductor’s monthly revenue growth; a drop below 10% year-over-year would signal fading AI capex demand. The analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 stocks and Amplify CWP International Enhanced Dividend Income ETF wasn't one of them. Get them here FREE. The Amplify CWP International Enhanced Dividend Income ETF (NYSEARCA:IDVO) has quietly become one of the more interesting income vehicles in the international space, with the ETF returning 35% over the past year and almost 12% year-to-date. IDVO pairs ex-US dividend equities with covered calls to generate monthly income, and the fund has ridden a sharp run in semiconductor and materials names that dominate its top holdings. With IDVO trading near $42 after a 2% pullback over the past week, the question for the next 12 months is whether the income engine can keep up if the underlying winners cool off. IDVO holds roughly $445 million in net assets and carries an expense ratio of 0.65%, per the Amplify fact sheet dated May 4, 2026. The sub-advisor Capital Wealth Planning runs the fund actively, selecting international dividend payers and overlaying calls on individual names. The recent return profile has been driven less by dividends and more by capital appreciation in concentrated tech and materials positions: Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE:TSM) is up 106% over one year, ASML Holding (NASDAQ:ASML) is up 98%, and Southern Copper (NYSE:SCCO) is up 101%. That kind of move changes how a covered-call strategy behaves. The dominant macro lever for IDVO right now is the AI infrastructure spending cycle, because TSM, ASML, and Alibaba (NYSE:BABA) together anchor the portfolio's risk and return. ASML raised its 2026 revenue guidance to €36 billion to €40 billion, and CEO Christophe Fouquet said "demand for chips is outpacing supply" as customers accelerate capacity expansion. Alibaba's Cloud Intelligence Group revenue grew 40% year-over-year in the latest quarter with AI products at 30% of external cloud revenue. The signal to monitor is TSM's monthly revenue release, which the company publishes on the 10th of each month on its investor relations site. April 2026 monthly revenue grew almost 18% year-over-year, but TSM's most recent quarterly filing missed the $1 trillion revenue consensus. A second consecutive miss, or a TSM monthly print below 10% growth, would signal that the AI capex impulse driving IDVO's largest contributors is fading. Investors who watched the 2022 semiconductor downcycle remember how quickly capex deferrals flowed through to equipment names like ASML. The fund-specific lever is the volatility regime that determines covered-call income. The VIX sits at almost 18, in the 15 to 20 sweet spot where premiums are workable but not stressed. The year saw a March spike to almost 31 that would have generated elevated premiums for IDVO's writers. If the VIX compresses below 15, as it did at almost 14 in late 2025, monthly distributions face mathematical pressure because there is simply less premium to harvest. The more subtle issue is that TSM, ASML, and SCCO have all roughly doubled over twelve months. Covered-call writers on those names have likely been called away repeatedly, leaving IDVO with capped upside on its best performers. The signal to watch is the monthly distribution itself, posted on Amplify's IDVO product page. A sustained decline in the per-share distribution paired with rising NAV would confirm the cap is binding; a stable distribution with flat NAV would suggest the strategy is balanced. Watch TSM's monthly revenue prints for any break below 10% year-over-year growth as the cleanest read on whether the AI capex cycle anchoring IDVO's top holdings is still intact. Then watch the next two monthly distributions against the VIX trend: if volatility drifts toward 15 and distributions hold flat, the active managers are earning their fee. If both fall together, the income story weakens before the price chart shows it. This analyst's 2025 picks are up 106% on average. He just named his top 10 stocks to buy in 2026. Get them here FREE.

title: Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US) is no longer standing alone! As the era of AI inference unfolds, investment flows into new segments, with MediaTek, Samsung, and others emerging as new favorites. - 富途牛牛
content: After several consecutive years of surging as NVIDIA's top-performing “shadow stock” in Asian markets, $Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US)$ it is now increasingly competing with other artificial intelligence (AI) concept stocks for investor attention. As mainstream adoption of AI drives demand for hardware beyond NVIDIA’s high-end chips, equity traders are chasing a broader set of beneficiaries. Multiple AI sub-themes—from tightening supply of memory chips to advances in robotics—are also drawing capital inflows. Meanwhile, single-stock position limits are prompting funds to diversify their holdings. Retail investors, who have long been familiar with Taiwan Semiconductor through American Depositary Receipts (ADRs), now also have more alternative Asian tech stocks to choose from. As a result, Taiwan Semiconductor’s stock has underperformed MediaTek—a chip design company—by the widest margin since 2009 this year. At the same time, the market capitalization gap between Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung Electronics, the world’s largest memory chipmaker, has significantly narrowed, with the latter also joining the 'trillion-dollar market cap club.' Jason Hsu, Chief Investment Officer at Rayliant Global Advisors in Boston, stated that the market is witnessing a 'structural shift away from Taiwan Semiconductor toward other companies.' He added that newly raised fund capital 'is flowing disproportionately into other tech firms that are also benefiting from record AI-related capital expenditures.' Although Taiwan Semiconductor’s share price has risen 44% this year—supported by strong sales and earnings—it has lagged behind MediaTek and Samsung Electronics, whose shares have each gained nearly 150%. This mirrors NVIDIA’s situation: despite continued robust growth, its stock performance has started to trail some other AI-related equities. There is little doubt that Taiwan Semiconductor, as the manufacturer of virtually all of NVIDIA’s advanced GPUs (graphics processing units), will continue benefiting from AI demand for the foreseeable future. However, as AI increasingly shifts toward the 'inferencing' phase—focused on executing specific tasks—other players are emerging as new winners. Hot trades are emerging among chip design companies—for example, MediaTek is assisting Google in developing application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs). Meanwhile, demand is also rising for central processing units (CPUs), which are relatively less technologically demanding and can be manufactured not only by Taiwan Semiconductor but also by foundries operated by Samsung and Intel (INTC.US). Brian Ooi, Portfolio Manager at Swiss-Asia Financial Services Pte., said, 'Agent-based AI is broadening the scope of AI-related trades because AI agents require more CPUs.' He added, 'As AI spending shifts from the training phase to the inferencing phase, I expect this diffusion trend to persist and become the next leg of the AI trade.' Moreover, because Taiwan Semiconductor focuses on logic chips, it does not directly benefit from the current boom in memory and data storage devices—a trend that has driven significant share price gains for Samsung and its peers. Global investors will soon gain easier access to these memory-related equities, as South Korea’s SK Hynix and Japan’s Kioxia Holdings both plan to launch ADRs this year. Asian firms also feature prominently in the newly launched and popular Roundhill Memory ETF, and U.S. retail investors can now even trade Korean stocks directly online. Another reason for Taiwan Semiconductor’s relative underperformance is that many actively managed funds impose a 10% cap on single-stock holdings. Given that Taiwan Semiconductor now accounts for over 40% of the weight in the Taiwan Weighted Index, these funds are compelled to buy other stocks to keep pace with the benchmark index. Jian Shi Cortesi, a portfolio manager at GAM Investment Management in Zurich, said: 'I already hold a position in Taiwan Semiconductor close to 10%, and over the past few months, I have further increased allocations to **** tech stocks driven by AI demand.' She added that these companies include those engaged in chip packaging, power management, thermal solutions, and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Kevin Net, Head of Asian Equities at Financiere de l’Echiquier, noted that due to the 10% holding limit, his fund is 'structurally underweight Taiwan Semiconductor,' but has raised its 'non-Taiwan Semiconductor AI exposure' by 5% compared to earlier this year. He stated that his investment targets include MediaTek, Samsung Electronics, as well as Taiwan’s ASE Group and Chroma ATE, as these companies are also poised to benefit from Taiwan Semiconductor’s capital expenditures. Total assets of TWD 8.66 trillion (+21.42% YoY) against total liabilities of TWD 2.73 trillion (+7.78%) – the balance sheet is expanding faster on the asset side than the liability side, which is the right configuration for a business in capex investment mode. Return on assets at 19.86% and return on capital at 24.42% – those are not numbers that semiconductor cyclicals typically print. The structural read: TSMC is operating at near-monopoly economics inside the advanced-node segment. The ~70% global foundry market share is structurally locked in by the technology gap between TSM and the field – Samsung and Intel Foundry are still measurably behind on both yield and node leadership, even as both publicly position to close the gap. The bull case requires gross margin expansion. The bear case argues it's already topped. Q1 FY2026 gross margin printed at 66.2% – an extraordinary level for any contract manufacturer in any cycle. Mid-2026 peak guidance is 67.5%. The Street consensus model bakes in continued expansion toward 70% by FY2028 on the back of N3 depreciation roll-off, yield maturation, the move into N2/A16, the avoidance of ASML's $400 million High-NA EUV tools, and an HPC mix shift with ASP price hikes. Here's the problem: TSMC's CFO Wendell Huang has explicitly guided that overseas fab ramp-up will dilute gross margins by 2%-3% in FY2026 and 3%-4% in the latter half of the decade. The $20 billion Arizona expansion approved by the board in May 2026 is the structural margin tax that doesn't go away. Combine that with the depreciation arbitrage strategy – delaying High-NA EUV adoption until FY2029 and using extreme multi-patterning on existing Low-NA EUV tools to hit N2/A16 densities – and the math gets uncomfortable: multi-patterning increases wafer cycle times and creates throughput bottlenecks, which caps absolute wafer output even as margin per wafer holds up. The realistic gross margin range is 66%-67% as a plateau, not a base camp for further expansion. Any model assuming 70%+ by FY2028 is mathematically optimistic in the face of the overseas tax plus the throughput cap. The growth engine is unambiguous. TSMC's HPC segment – which captures AI accelerators, advanced server chips, and the data-center silicon that runs the entire generative AI buildout – is the dominant revenue driver and the highest-margin mix in the business. Demand for silicon chips is scaling in lockstep with demand for AI compute, and TSM is the singular supplier for the bleeding-edge nodes that the AI complex depends on. Nvidia's Q1 FY2026 print of $81.62 billion in revenue (+85% YoY) with net profit more than tripling to $58.3 billion is functionally a TSM print – Nvidia doesn't manufacture; TSMC does. The same applies to Apple, Broadcom, and Qualcomm, which together with Nvidia constitute the customer concentration risk and the customer concentration tailwind in equal measure. The FY2026 revenue growth expectation sits at approximately 32% YoY, above management's own guidance, with HPC carrying disproportionate weight in that mix. The consensus FY2026 EPS estimate is $15.61 (+46.57% YoY), and FY2027 is $19.52 (+25.03% YoY). That's a long-term EPS CAGR (3-5 year) of 31.44%, which is the growth rate the market has to justify against the valuation. The flip side of being the indispensable supplier is that the customers know they're concentrated. Apple is exploring both Intel and Samsung as backup foundry options, not because either is better today, but because supply chain resilience post-Trump-tariff regime is now boardroom-level policy. Elon Musk's Terafab is reportedly working with Intel Foundry, which is exactly the kind of high-profile second-source validation that gives Intel a credible runway to chase the segment. These are not near-term threats to TSMC's 70% market share – but they represent the first credible signals that the foundry monopoly is being actively eroded at the design-win stage, even before it shows up in revenue numbers. By FY2028-FY2029, that competitive dynamic matters more than it does today. This is the variable that flips the whole bull case. Approximately 45% of U.S. data center projects slated for FY2026 are running delayed or canceled – not because of chip supply, but because of grid power constraints, utility limitations, and zoning opposition to megawatt-guzzling AI facilities. That's the inventory bullwhip risk nobody on the bull side wants to underwrite: TSMC is adding three new N3 fabs to the Tainan GIGAFAB cluster for H1 FY2027, the Arizona buildout is accelerating, FY2026 capex was raised to the $52 billion–$56 billion high end, and yet the downstream physical infrastructure that absorbs all that AI silicon is hitting hard limits. If hyperscalers can't physically plug in the Nvidia Blackwell, Rubin SuperPODs, and Broadcom-designed Google TPU 8t/8i chips that are currently rolling off TSMC's 3nm lines, the order pace decelerates meaningfully in late FY2026 and through FY2027. The market is pricing TSMC on semiconductor supply; the actual constraint is energy and real estate absorption. That mismatch is the single biggest unpriced risk in the stock. The CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) packaging dominance is the moat that the market has finally figured out, but the next leg is more meaningful. By FY2028, TSMC will deploy 14-reticle CoWoS capable of integrating 10 massive compute dies and 20 HBM stacks into a single package. The bigger story is TSMC-COUPE (Compact Universal Photonic Engine), entering production in FY2026, which integrates a 200Gbps micro-ring modulator directly inside the package – delivering 10x latency reduction and 2x power efficiency versus traditional pluggable optics. The structural implication: TSMC is solving the AI interconnect bottleneck through silicon photonics. By FY2029, the rollout of the 40-reticle SoW-X (System-on-Wafer) lets TSM print entire server subsystems on a single wafer. That changes the addressable market from the ~$100 billion foundry TAM into the much larger optical transceiver, networking, and system integration TAM – which is the case for a structural P/E re-rating from a semiconductor manufacturer multiple (10-year average ~22.66x) to an AI-infrastructure single-seller multiple (30x+). That's the long-term catalyst that isn't yet priced into the current $403 print. TSMC's FY2026 capex range of $52-$56 billion is the most aggressive in foundry history. Three new N3 fabs are being added to Tainan for H1 FY2027. The Arizona expansion got a $20 billion injection in May 2026. The April 2026 agreement with Northland Power to offtake 100% of the 1,022 MW Hai Long offshore wind project for 30 years is the energy-security play to insulate Taiwan operations from geopolitical shocks (think: 2026 Iran conflict disrupting LNG/Helium logistics). All of this is rational management. None of it is cheap. The depreciation load is going to grow meaningfully through FY2027-FY2028, and the margin offsets (depreciation arbitrage on existing tools) only buy time, not permanent escape. The valuation math works in TSM's favor – but with strict ceilings. At the current $403 print, forward P/E (FY2026) of 25.9x versus 5-year average TTM P/E of 24.72x says the stock isn't cheap but isn't extended either. Applied to the FY2027 consensus EPS of $19.52 with a slightly discounted 24x multiple (accounting for the 3%-4% overseas margin tax), the fair value lands at $468.48 – an 18.3% upside from current levels. The Wall Street average target sits at $467.84, validating that math. On the PEG framework: TSM's forward PEG of 0.83x signals the market is applying a meaningful geopolitical and cyclical discount to the growth. A pure 1x PEG on the 31.44% EPS CAGR justifies a 31.44x P/E – which gets you to a FY2027 absolute ceiling of $613.70 (55% upside), in line with the highest bull-case target of $600. Discount that to a more conservative 0.8x PEG and the implied P/E is 25.15x, yielding a FY2027 PEG-adjusted target of ~$491 (24% upside). The risk-adjusted bear scenario: if the 45% data center delay rate triggers a 15% downward revision in FY2027 EPS (even at one-third impact), adjusted FY2027 EPS of $16.59 at an AI-cyclical-low 20x multiple gives you a $331.80 risk-adjusted target (16.2% downside). That's the asymmetry that defines the trade. The price structure on TSM is constructive but not screaming breakout. The stock is sitting at $403.79 inside a $385-$420 trading range that has held for the better part of a month. The all-time high at $421.97 is the primary resistance that the bulls need to clear with conviction. Above $421.97, the open air targets $440-$450 fast on a measured-move basis. Below $385, the next demand zone sits at $370 and then $355 as the 200-day moving average band. A clean break of the $385 floor on weekly volume opens $355-$365 as the structural retest. Momentum reads: the recent push to $419.50 in early May (per the 1-year chart) was followed by a roughly 7% pullback to $385.61, with the current $403 print as the recovery attempt. The pattern is a higher-low structure inside a broadly bullish trend that has the stock up ~112% from the 52-week low. Daily RSI is moderate – not overbought, not oversold. The Wall Street consensus has not chased the stock higher post-Q1, which tells you positioning is digesting the move rather than extending it. The single most important variable for TSM over the next four quarters isn't its own execution – it's the capex commitments of Microsoft (MSFT), Meta (META), Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOG/GOOGL), Apple (AAPL), Nvidia (NVDA), AMD, and Broadcom (AVGO). If those names continue to ratify $300+ billion in aggregate annual AI infrastructure spend, TSM's order book stays full and margin expansion math works. If any one of them dials back guidance citing power constraints, ROI uncertainty, or model commoditization, the downstream impact on TSM is immediate. Nvidia's recent print confirms demand is there at the chip level; the question is whether the demand survives the physical absorption bottleneck through 2027. The PEG-implied discount in TSM's valuation has a name: Taiwan Strait risk. A Chinese blockade scenario isn't priced as a base case, but it's the persistent overhang that explains why TSM trades at 25x forward versus an AI-infrastructure-pure-play multiple closer to 35x-40x. The 2026 Iran conflict has reminded markets that supply chain disruption isn't theoretical – which is part of why TSMC is paying premium prices for offshore wind contracts and accelerating the Arizona buildout. The geopolitical discount in TSM doesn't go away as long as the cross-strait status remains contested, and that's a structural ceiling on the multiple that no execution can fully neutralize. The bull case on TSM breaks if any of the following land: hyperscaler capex guidance cuts in the next earnings cycle (MSFT, META, GOOG, AMZN); the U.S. data center delay rate moves above 50%, confirming the absorption bottleneck; a clean break below $385 that opens the $355 region; Apple or another tier-1 customer announces a meaningful Intel Foundry or Samsung supply agreement that materially reduces TSM's 70% market share assumption; Taiwan Strait tensions escalate to the point where the geopolitical discount widens; or the gross margin guidance for late FY2026 prints below 66%, confirming the margin plateau thesis sooner than expected. Any two of these in combination triggers a multiple compression toward 20x forward and the $331 risk-adjusted floor. The bullish read gets fully confirmed on: a clean breakout above $421.97 to new all-time highs with volume; mid-FY2026 gross margin guidance lifted toward 68%; continued hyperscaler capex upside revisions through Q2-Q3 FY2026; a credible deescalation in U.S.-Iran tensions that removes the broader macro overlay; CoWoS capacity expansion delivering ahead of schedule to support the AI silicon ramp; or early TSMC-COUPE deployment validation that pulls forward the silicon-photonics catalyst from FY2029 into FY2027. Any of these triggers the run toward $467-$491. The broader semiconductor tape is mixed today. Nvidia (NVDA) at $219.47 (-1.79%) despite the earnings beat. Broadcom (AVGO) at $414.90 (+0.68%). Micron (MU) at $744.50 (+1.71%). AMD softer, Intel (INTC) at $116.41 (-2.14%). SanDisk (SNDK) jumping +6.82% to $1,487.50. The relative-strength signal for TSM at +0.50% while NVDA bleeds is meaningful – it suggests the foundry is being treated as the lower-beta way to play AI infrastructure when the high-multiple names get pressured. That defensive AI bid for TSM is exactly the kind of rotation that supports the medium-term thesis. The Fed's hawkish pivot (62% odds of a December hike), the 10-year at 4.615%, and the DXY at 99.4 are not stock-bullish inputs in aggregate. But TSM specifically has a USD revenue base that is partially hedged by the weaker TWD and Asian export economics. The currency mix actually works modestly in TSM's favor in a stronger-dollar regime, which is a wrinkle worth noting versus pure-USD revenue names. The bigger macro risk is multiple compression across the semiconductor space if yields rip higher – a 10-year at 4.8%+ would compress the entire chip group's forward multiples and pull TSM down with it regardless of execution. The call: TSM is a BUY on pullbacks into the $385-$395 zone, with a primary target of $468 (18% upside) and a stretch target of $491 (PEG-adjusted, 24% upside). The stock is a HOLD at current levels ($400-$420), where the risk/reward is balanced and the upside requires a fresh catalyst (Q2 print, hyperscaler capex upside, CoWoS news). The trade is to ROTATE OUT of long positions into the $468-$490 zone, front-running the FY2027 inventory correction risk that the bull case has not yet priced. This is a BULLISH read with structural caveats. The thesis is supported by: the 50%+ net margin print, the 35% revenue growth, the dominant ~70% foundry market share, the AI infrastructure tailwind, the CoWoS/COUPE/SoW-X long-term packaging moat, the conservative valuation at 25x forward, the 0.83x PEG suggesting discounted growth pricing, and the relative strength versus high-beta AI names. The thesis is constrained by: the gross margin plateau at 66%-67%, the 3%-4% overseas dilution tax, the 45% U.S. data center delay rate, the customer concentration risk with Apple/Intel exposure, the multi-patterning throughput cap, the geopolitical Taiwan Strait discount, and the $20 billion Arizona capex drag. The catalyst path: a clean break above $421.97 opens $440-$450, with the structural target at $468-$491. A break below $385 opens $355-$365, with the risk-adjusted floor at $331. The market sits in a $35 range between those triggers, and the breakout is fundamental (next earnings print, hyperscaler capex guidance, gross margin trajectory) rather than technical. Add on pullbacks, trim at $468-$490, and respect $385 as the line where the thesis gets retested. The AI silicon story is real, the foundry moat is real, the margin profile is best-in-class – but the downstream absorption risk is the variable that turns a 24% upside trade into a 16% downside trade if the macro/grid catalyst lands badly. Constructive with disciplined position management is the only honest read on where TSM sits today.

title: TSM launches osu ai for automated Minecraft building - VPEsports
content: The TSM organization, representing North America, recently presented its new product, an application. osu.ai , which introduces artificial intelligence directly into the cubic expanses of Minecraft. The idea is simple — players can now build buildings in survival mode by simply sending text commands to a neural network that builds objects in the open world. In addition to the construction site itself, the application for the Java version allows, by the way, to change the skins of characters and textures of the environment – it’s interesting, really. However, the reaction of the community turned out to be, let’s say, far from enthusiastic, and the club immediately received a barrage of criticism from loyal fans. Many fans have openly stated that this approach kills the main feature of the game. “This goes against the foundation of Minecraft” — this is how angry comments on social networks sound, where people are sure that the whole point of the project lies in personal creativity, and not in soulless scripts. It is strange to see such a move from TSM now — the organization is now actively reshaping its structure. Let me remind you that just recently, on February 1, the club dispersed its Apex Legends roster — the guys took only the seventh place at the ALGS Year 5 Championship, which was held in January. Before that, there was a departure from the VALORANT discipline. There, the team finished second at the VCT Ascension Americas, but in the end, after losing to ENVY, they couldn’t jump into the top division of the VCT Americas — it’s probably a shame. But there are also positive developments — TSM has recently officially joined the 12 partner teams in the new Marvel Rivals discipline. In addition, the club is firmly embedded in The Finals shooter partner. At the first Grand Major, the organization, by the way, clung to fifth place and snatched $3,750 (about 2,757 pounds) in prize money – a good result to start with. In general, the topic of neural networks in esports is currently at its peak. For example, on February 4, the Sentinels club, together with Theta Network, launched their AI bot for support – it advises fans on tournaments and lineups, which is quite convenient. Even at CES 2026, Razer did not stay away — they showed Project AVA. This is an AI-based esports coach who analyzes your skill in real time and gives advice right during the rink — powerful, isn’t it? As a result, we see that TSM is trying to find new growth points, but they clearly missed the Minecraft audience — the players do not want to give their creativity to algorithms. To be honest, the question of where the help ends and the outright “abuse” begins is now an issue in the community. Gamers are tirelessly arguing whether it is overstepping osu.ai the invisible line behind which creativity turns into mechanical deception. This software takes over all the thrust in Minecraft and similar projects, which instantly highlights the problem of bans and jeopardizes the very concept of fair play on popular servers. By the way, if you delve into mechanics, automation is always a risk that, apparently, many underestimate. If we take classic Minecraft, then any third—party application that automates tapping or construction — whether it’s a fancy AI or a good old autoclicker – is interpreted by the officials as interference with the client. In fact, this is a direct ticket to the ban list for using cheats. However, the situation varies on public platforms: if you are “demolished” on Hypixel in no time, then on some anarchic servers the moderators overlook this until an anti-cheat like NoCheatPlus starts sounding the alarm. It should be understood that in PvP arenas, the use of osu.ai it is almost one hundred percent likely to be considered an “unfair advantage”. The speed of clicks and the accuracy of positioning here obviously break the balance, causing fierce rage among the community and a pack of reporters. However, if you dig into creativity or on a closed server with a couple of friends, the risk is minimal — everything there, in general, is based on personal sympathies, and not on Microsoft’s rigid guidelines. In single mode, the use of neural networks remains, in fact, a matter of your inner conscience, because you do not harm others. But in surviving with friends, everything is decided by collective agreements — otherwise, a toxic atmosphere and resentment cannot be avoided. In a competitive environment, any manifestation of automation is a guaranteed conflict, mutation, or eternal lockdown, because the Minecraft community filters such “innovations” extremely harshly. Interestingly, amid these software scandals, esports giants continue to experiment with the introduction of AI into the training structure itself.

title: Marvel Rivals Ignite 2026: Liquid and TSM Join the Battle - VPEsports
content: Publisher NetEase Games has finally revealed the cards on the list of partner organizations for the upcoming Marvel Rivals Ignite 2026 season. In the latest issue of Dev Vision, dedicated to update 6.5, twelve clubs have been highlighted — here are the mastodons of the industry, and very fresh blood. Virtus.pro By the way, they are returning to the ranks as the current champions of the 2025 Grand Final to try to keep the crown. In truth, the competition will be wild: the list also includes the winners of the American Invitational 100 Thieves, as well as Sentinels, FlyQuest and, of course, Natus Vincere. Asia is also in place — the Gen.G Esports and REJECT brands, which were hacked back in the first season, are back in business. Interestingly, the 2026 season has attracted new heavyweights. Apparently, Team Heretics from Spain, as well as North American Spacestation Gaming, along with the legendary TSM, joined the project. Powerful, don’t you think? The cherry on the cake lies in high-profile collaborations. The Citadel Gaming team — and these are, for a second, the tops of Europe — will now perform under the Liquid Citadel tag after the deal with Team Liquid. At the same time, NRG decided to join forces with San Francisco Shock by forming the NRG Shock alliance — hello Overwatch fans, it’s going to be hot. To be honest, many fans were stunned by ENVY‘s absence. The finalists of the 2025 mid-season faded into the shadows back in November and still remain deathly silent — a rather alarming sign. Plus, the Chinese leaders from OUG, who took the first stages of Ignite last year, were not on the list. Where DarkZero, Crazy Raccoon and Rad Esports went is also a big question, because these guys were the face of the scene. In general, the partner roster looks solid, but there are still questions about NetEase Games. The financial side of the issue this season looks even more intriguing than just the distribution of the prize money. In addition to direct payments, partner teams are actually embedded in the economy of the game itself through a system of revenue sharing from customization. The same case with an exclusive skin from Virtus.pro — this is just the tip of the iceberg, to be honest. NetEase Games plans to turn esports assets into the main driver of monetization, which, in truth, will provide clubs with tremendous stability even with temporary drawdowns in results. But don’t think that this is just a “one—way ticket” – the system is extremely rigid. The interesting thing here is that protection from relegation, which is so much debated, actually has its limits, and partner status does not guarantee eternal life on Olympus. If the team starts openly “draining” the distance, no amount of old achievements will save it from pressure from hungry applicants from open qualifications. Championship points, which are now being farmed by everyone without exception, create the very “death zone” where any mistake can cost a place on the final lan of the year. And here’s the most interesting thing: while some are enjoying the cosmetic bonuses, others are already preparing the ground for the most high-profile comeback in the history of the discipline. Actually, it is this contrast between the “protected” giants and the audacious newcomers that brings us to the main question.: Which of the legends from last season suddenly found themselves overboard from the celebration of life? The Marvel Rivals Ignite 2026 season unfolds according to a tight schedule: after Preseason and Stage 1, Mid-Season Finals are waiting for us, followed by Stage 2. The final point is the Grand Finals in November. NetEase Games publisher has clearly raised the bar by increasing the number of LAN events and inflating the prize pool to $1,000,000. The teams are now fighting not just for a check, but for the right to enter the history of this multiverse. The meta promises to be aggressive: bundles from Phoenix, Blade and Venom force us to reconsider the very essence of the synergy of roles. The main Marvel Rivals Ignite 2026 show starts in mid-November and ends in early December. Twelve of the best bands on the planet will meet at the LAN Arena in Atlanta. The rules are strict: a group stage with two pools of 6 participants, a cross-grid in the quarterfinals and a Bo5 format in the decisive stages. Any mistake in the timing of the ultimate — and the favorite goes home, as happened with Navi and FlyQuest last year. The pressure level here is exorbitant, because the status of the strongest in the world is at stake. Team Liquid and Sentinels now look the most stable, which confirms their positions in the current power ranking. After completing Stage 2, their winrate in high-level matches is astounding, and the combo realization rate (PP%) consistently stays above 85%. These organizations rely on proven Hulk and Doctor Strange, which allows them to dictate terms within the framework of the current patch 6.5. While competitors are looking for themselves, these giants simply take their own due to the discipline and depth of the hero pool. FlyQuest and Virtus.pro — teams that have already proved their worth by closing Navi 2-0 in the 2025 semifinals. Their strength lies in the work of the special teams: Rocket Raccoon provides control, and Star-Lord is responsible for the lightning push. Their defense statistics in the minority (penalty kill) exceed 88%. By the start of Ignite 2026, they had conducted a series of transfers to ensure that they would skip Stage 2 and gain a foothold in the Grand Finals bracket. The pressure of these guys can be a problem even for the ranking leaders. Gaimin Gladiators entered Marvel Rivals, taking with them a pragmatic approach typical of their success in other disciplines. Their tactics are based around protection: Jeff the Land Shark in the role of a tank gives an HD-SV% indicator (protection from dangerous attacks) at 90%. While the young talents at Penny Parker are tearing apart the flanks, the analytical staff is calculating every move of the opponent. If the Gladiators keep up the pace in the Mid-Season Finals, we will see a serious distortion in the usual hierarchy of forces. Navi, the triumphants of Ignite 2025, still remember the defeat of FlyQuest in Bo5. Their championship path in October and November was based on the impeccable links of Wolverine and Cloak & Dagger. The organization is currently focused on adapting to Patch 6.5, where melee heroes have received significant enhancements. All the past experience and the Cap + Rocket bundle are aimed at one goal — to return to the Grand Finals and prove that last year’s misfire was an accident. Clubs with the status of NetEase Games partners enjoy the best seeding and release branded skins, but this does not always help on the server. Their strong point is quick plays, but they often sag in long matches. A penalty kill score below 80% indicates problems with self-control. In the 2026 Grand Finals bracket, they will most likely have to wait at the bottom, unless the Blade transfer corrects the damage situation in the decisive skirmishes. The formation of lineups like Cloud9 around the Hulk duo and Emma Frost in a support position creates a new reality. These super-timers are effective where perfect first pass and high performance (G/60) are required. Update 6.5 makes their strategies with Ultron and Doctor Doom virtually invulnerable to standard counterpicks. When a star plays in each position, individual skill begins to outweigh any tactical preparations of the opponents. Patch 6.5 has completely reshaped the Ignite 2026 landscape. Abyss Awakens buffs for Phoenix and Blade have shifted the focus towards dive-meta, where the speed of movement destroys slow tanks. The chaos of the past years is giving way to a structured game (ordered play). The effectiveness of most combinations has increased by 15%, but the outcome of Bo5 still depends on the quality of the penalty kill. The same Team Liquid is already adjusting Star-Lord to the synergy with Venom, realizing: Whoever can master HD-SV% faster in high-risk areas will take the crown of the Grand Final.

title: Is TSMC Still a Strong Buy Amidst Hedge Fund Trims - Kavout
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) finds itself at a fascinating crossroads, commanding a $2.05 trillion market capitalization as of May 18, 2026, yet navigating a landscape where some prominent institutional investors are taking profits. The stock is currently trading at $395.95, down 2.08% today, but still near its 52-week high of $421.97. Despite this recent dip, the overwhelming sentiment from Wall Street analysts remains bullish, with a consensus "Buy" rating. This dichotomy—strong analyst conviction juxtaposed with strategic portfolio adjustments by major funds—presents a nuanced picture for investors. The core of the bull case rests firmly on TSMC's indispensable role in the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, acting as the sole foundry for many of the most advanced chips powering this transformative technology. However, the recent Q1 2026 13F filings reveal that even high-conviction investors like Philippe Laffont's Coatue Management and Daniel Loeb's Third Point have significantly trimmed their TSM holdings. Coatue, for instance, slashed its TSM stake by approximately 83%, reducing its value to $197.64 billion in Q1 2026. Similarly, Third Point reduced its position by 19.68% in Q4 2025, retaining 1.43 million shares. These moves, while substantial in dollar terms, are largely interpreted as tactical profit-taking after an extraordinary run-up, rather than a fundamental loss of faith in TSMC's long-term prospects. The question for investors now is whether these trims signal a broader caution or simply prudent portfolio rebalancing in a high-flying sector. Wall Street's view on TSMC remains overwhelmingly positive, with a strong consensus "Buy" rating. According to MarketBeat data from May 11, 2026, 15 analysts cover TSM, with 11 "Buy" ratings and 2 "Strong Buy" ratings. Only a single "Hold" rating exists among the 5 analysts tracked by WallStreetZen, with no "Sell" recommendations. This robust endorsement is reflected in the average 12-month price target, which stands at $420.00 according to WallStreetZen, implying a +6.07% upside from the current price of $395.95. MarketBeat offers a slightly lower average target of $404.29, still indicating positive appreciation. Individual analyst updates further reinforce this bullish outlook. Needham, for example, recently raised its price target to a sector-leading $480.00 on May 11, 2026, a significant jump from its earlier $410.00 target set on January 15, 2026. DA Davidson reiterated a $450.00 target, first set on February 13, 2026, and reaffirmed on May 11, 2026. Bank of America also reiterated a "Buy" rating with a $470.00 price target as of March 15, 2026, citing stronger-than-expected first-quarter sales driven by AI demand. These high targets suggest that some analysts believe TSMC still has considerable room to run, even after its impressive performance over the past year, which saw the stock surge from a 52-week low of $188.81. The range of price targets, from a low of $330.00 (Bernstein, December 8, 2025) to a high of $480.00, highlights the varying degrees of optimism, but the median target of $405.00 (from 6 analysts over the last 6 months, per Quiver Quantitative) indicates a general expectation of continued upward momentum. This strong analyst sentiment is largely predicated on TSMC's critical role in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, particularly for high-performance computing and AI chips. The company's technological leadership and capacity expansion plans are seen as key drivers for future revenue growth and profitability, justifying the premium valuation. The insatiable demand for artificial intelligence (AI) chips is unequivocally the primary catalyst propelling TSMC's current and projected growth. As the world's leading pure-play foundry, TSMC is the exclusive manufacturer of the most advanced processors from industry giants like Nvidia and AMD, including Nvidia's cutting-edge Blackwell GPUs and AMD's upcoming next-generation GPUs. This pivotal position in the AI ecosystem ensures a robust pipeline of orders for TSMC's advanced nodes, such as 3nm and 2nm technologies. The company's first-quarter sales for 2026 were notably stronger than expected, a direct consequence of this surging AI demand, as highlighted by BofA's reiterated "Buy" rating in March 2026. This AI-driven demand is also translating into massive capital spending by TSMC. The company is investing heavily to expand its manufacturing capacity for advanced nodes, anticipating sustained growth in the high-performance computing (HPC) sector. While specific Q1 2026 capital expenditure figures were not provided, the strong analyst sentiment noted by Finviz in February 2026 explicitly linked "massive 2026 capital spending" to AI demand. Such investments are crucial for TSMC to maintain its technological lead and meet the escalating requirements of its key customers, who are themselves racing to develop more powerful AI hardware. The market chatter, as tracked by Quiver Quantitative, underscores the anticipation of "tighter capacity at advanced nodes," signaling that TSMC's production capabilities will remain highly sought after. The strategic importance of TSMC's technology extends beyond just GPUs. Its fabrication processes are essential for a wide array of AI-related hardware, from specialized AI accelerators to high-bandwidth memory interfaces. This broad exposure across the AI value chain solidifies TSMC's long-term growth prospects, making it a critical infrastructure play for investors looking to capitalize on the AI boom. The company's ability to consistently deliver leading-edge process technology positions it as an indispensable partner for innovation in the rapidly evolving AI landscape. An examination of institutional ownership data for TSMC in Q1 2026 reveals a dynamic, albeit slightly cautious, landscape. As of May 18, 2026, TSMC is held by 3,313 institutional investors, a modest increase of 79 holders from the prior quarter. However, the overall institutional ownership percentage saw a slight dip of 0.76 percentage points, bringing it to 14.5% of outstanding shares. The total invested capital by institutions stands at a substantial $252.32 billion. This indicates that while more funds are initiating positions, some larger players are rebalancing their exposure. Delving deeper into the activity, Q1 2026 saw 311 new positions established, 1,584 funds increasing their stakes, 1,223 funds reducing their holdings, and 250 funds completely closing out their positions. This mixed activity suggests a nuanced approach from institutional investors. While the number of funds increasing their stakes significantly outweighs those reducing or closing, the slight decrease in overall ownership percentage implies that the average size of new or increased positions might be smaller, or that larger reductions by a few key players had a more pronounced impact. For instance, Coatue Management's substantial 83% trim in Q1 2026, reducing its TSM holding to $197.64 billion, would certainly contribute to this trend. Top holders like FMR LLC (60.39 million shares, $20.41 billion) and Sanders Capital, LLC (28.06 million shares, $9.48 billion) slightly reduced their stakes by 1.2% and 12.2% respectively. Conversely, CAPITAL WORLD INVESTORS significantly increased its holding by 20.0% to 32.89 million shares ($11.11 billion), and SUSQUEHANNA INTERNATIONAL GROUP, LLP boosted its position by 23.7% to 19.40 million shares ($6.56 billion). The put/call ratio also saw a notable decrease of 58.6% from the prior quarter to 1.22, suggesting a reduction in bearish hedging activity or an increase in bullish option positions. Over the last 24 months, institutional buying totaled 101.12 million shares ($27.33 billion), while selling amounted to 110.95 million shares ($31.38 billion), indicating a slight net outflow of shares, consistent with the overall ownership percentage decline. Investing in TSMC, despite its dominant market position and critical role in AI, is not without its risks. Geopolitical tensions, particularly concerning Taiwan's relationship with mainland China, represent a significant overhang. Any escalation could severely disrupt TSMC's operations and the global semiconductor supply chain, given that the vast majority of its advanced manufacturing facilities are located on the island. While the company is expanding its global footprint with new fabs in Arizona and Japan, these efforts will take years to significantly diversify its production base. Another key risk lies in the cyclical nature of the semiconductor industry. While AI demand currently provides a strong tailwind, a broader economic downturn could impact overall chip demand, even for advanced nodes. Furthermore, the intense capital expenditure required to maintain technological leadership (as evidenced by "massive 2026 capital spending" driven by AI demand) can strain free cash flow in periods of slower growth. Competition, though currently limited at the leading edge, could intensify if rivals like Samsung Foundry or Intel's foundry services make significant technological strides. However, the opportunities for TSMC remain compelling. Its unparalleled technological leadership in advanced process nodes provides a deep moat, making it virtually irreplaceable for companies developing cutting-edge AI, HPC, and smartphone chips. The long-term secular growth trend in AI, cloud computing, and next-generation connectivity ensures a sustained demand for its services. TSMC's consistent execution, strong customer relationships, and strategic capacity expansions position it to capture a significant share of this growth. The company's ability to command premium pricing for its advanced technologies also supports robust margins. For investors, TSM offers a relatively de-risked way to play the AI boom, as it supplies the foundational technology to a broad array of AI innovators, rather than being reliant on the success of a single end-product. TSMC's current valuation, trading at $395.95 with an average analyst price target of $420.00, suggests a modest upside in the near term. However, its strategic importance and technological moat position it as a long-term compounder within the critical semiconductor industry. While institutional profit-taking warrants attention, the underlying demand drivers and analyst conviction paint a picture of continued strength. Investors should consider TSM a core holding for diversified exposure to the enduring growth of artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. Want deeper research on any stock?
